questions.q: You list Gemini, GPT, Claude and Llama. What actually separates them?
questions.a: Three are closed weights behind an API. The parameters are never published, and the only way to use them is to send text to somebody's server. Llama is open weights. You download the parameters and run the model on your own hardware. That difference changes an architecture rather than a preference. It decides whether data leaves your network. It decides whether you pay per token or per GPU hour. It decides whether the system can work offline or inside a network that forbids sending data out. Capability rankings move every few months. The deployment property does not, so lead with it.
questions.flag: Ranking them by benchmark. The ranking will be stale before the offer letter, and it tells the interviewer nothing about how you would choose.

teach.title: Where each named thing is actually evidenced

questions.q: What does “open weights” mean, and how is it not open source?
questions.a: A model is billions of numbers learned during training. Open weights means those numbers are published, so you can download them and run the model yourself. What that buys is the option to run offline, on your own GPUs, or inside a network that forbids outbound calls. No API-only model can do those at all. What you do not get is the training data, the training code, or an unrestricted licence. Most of these come with conditions on scale and on use. So it buys self-hosting and privacy. It does not buy the ability to rebuild the model or fully audit what went into it.
questions.flag: Using open source and open weights interchangeably. The distinction is a licensing fact, and legal teams in regulated industries ask about it first.

teach.title: The boundary worth defending

questions.q: What is a context window, and why not just use a huge one?
questions.a: It is the total number of tokens the model can look at in one go, prompt and reply together. Anything outside it does not exist as far as the model is concerned. Frontier models now reach about a million tokens, which is a large book. What that buys is a hard, checkable limit to design against. You can measure your prompt and know in advance whether it fits, instead of discovering truncation in production. The reason not to fill it is that you pay for every token and wait for every token. Attention also thins in the middle of a very long context. A big window is not a replacement for retrieving the right thing.
questions.flag: “Long context makes RAG obsolete.” It changes the cost curve. It does not change the fact that you still have to choose what goes in.

teach.title: What an agent actually is

questions.q: What is temperature, and does zero give you determinism?
questions.a: At each step the model produces a probability for every possible next token, and something has to choose one. Temperature controls how much that choice may wander. Near zero it almost always takes the most likely token. Higher values flatten the distribution and let unlikely ones through. What it buys is one dial moving output between reliable and varied, which are genuinely different jobs. Extraction, routing and scoring all want the low end. But zero does not give determinism. Batch composition, hardware and floating-point ordering still move results between runs. If you need reproducibility, record the outputs. A setting is not a guarantee.
questions.flag: Promising reproducible output from temperature zero. It is a common claim and it is wrong, and this is a question people ask precisely to see who repeats it.

questions.q: What is a system prompt, and what is it not?
questions.a: Text placed at the very front of the conversation, setting the model's role, its rules and its output format. It is marked differently from user turns and weighted more heavily. Underneath, it is still just text in the same context window. What it buys is behaviour set once rather than repeated in every request, and a single place to change it. What it is not is a security boundary. Anything arriving later in the context can argue with it and sometimes win. Untrusted text in the context is exactly the prompt-injection problem. Rules you must actually enforce belong in code.
questions.flag: Describing a prompt as a guardrail. A guardrail is something the model cannot get past, and a paragraph of instructions is not that.

questions.q: A model is not doing what you want. Prompt, retrieve, or fine-tune?
questions.a: In that order, and for different faults. Prompting fixes instructions it is not following, and costs one edit. Retrieval fixes facts it does not have, and the facts stay current because they live outside the model. Fine-tuning continues training on your examples so the weights change, and it fixes behaviour and output format you cannot get any other way. LoRA makes it cheap by freezing the original weights and training small added matrices. What that buys is style that sticks without being restated, and a shorter prompt. The classic mistake is fine-tuning to teach facts. The model learns the shape of your facts without learning the facts.
questions.flag: Naming fine-tuning first. It is the most expensive option with the slowest feedback loop, and the interviewer is checking whether you know that.

questions.q: What actually drives the bill on an agent system?
questions.a: Tokens, multiplied by the number of calls. A token is a chunk of text about three quarters of a word, and everything is priced in them. An agent loop re-sends its history every turn, so the cost grows faster than the conversation does. Output tokens usually cost several times more than input, which makes a verbose response format genuinely expensive. Knowing the unit is what lets you predict a bill before running anything. The lever that matters most is how many calls a run makes. That is why a fixed sequence beats a loop deciding for itself.
questions.flag: Quoting a per-token price as the answer. The multiplier is the call count, and that is an architecture decision rather than a vendor one.

questions.q: What is an agent?
questions.a: A model in a loop with tools. It is given a set of functions, it proposes a call, your code runs it, and the result goes back in. Then it decides again. Without the loop and the tools it is just a prompt with a nice name.
questions.flag: Defining it by autonomy or goals. Those are properties of some agents. The loop and the tools are what make it one at all.

teach.title: What an agent actually is

questions.q: When a model calls a function, who executes it?
questions.a: My code does. The model emits a request naming a function and its arguments. My process decides whether to honour that, runs it, and returns the result. The model never touches anything directly, which is why every tool call is a place I can validate, log or refuse.
questions.flag: Saying the model executes it. This is the single most revealing misconception in LLM interviews, because the whole security model follows from it.

teach.title: What an agent actually is

questions.q: Why does a tool's description matter so much?
questions.a: Because the description is the interface. The model chooses a tool by reading it, so a vague description means the tool gets used in the wrong situation. It is prompt text that behaves like an API contract, and it is edited far more casually than an API contract would be.
questions.flag: Treating descriptions as documentation. They are dispatch logic, and changing one changes behaviour.

questions.q: What makes your system multi-agent rather than three function calls?
questions.a: Honestly, in the vendor platform it is three function calls with one composer, and that is on purpose. What makes it worth the name is that each stage carries its own prompt, schema and model tier. What it deliberately is not is autonomous: they never call each other.
questions.flag: Defending the label. Conceding the structure and defending the constraint is a much stronger position, and it is the true one.

teach.title: The boundary worth defending

questions.q: Orchestration or choreography, and why?
questions.a: Orchestration, everywhere. One place holds the sequence, so there is one file to read and one place a deadline can live. Choreography spreads the control flow across components, which is fine for decoupled services and bad when you need to answer why the system did something.
questions.flag: Not knowing the pair of terms. They are the standard vocabulary for the exact choice you made.

teach.title: The boundary worth defending

questions.q: What did Google ADK actually give you?
questions.a: The loop, sub-agent sequencing, session state between iterations, and lifecycle hooks. Two specifics I would cite. LoopAgent with EventActions.escalate as the early exit, in the schematization retry loop. And a before_tool_callback in the lineage agent, used to make a precondition unskippable.
questions.flag: Listing features. Name the two hooks you used and what each one bought, or it sounds like a framework you read about.

teach.title: Where each named thing is actually evidenced

questions.q: What is MCP for?
questions.a: Describing a tool or data source once, in a standard shape, so any model client can use it without a bespoke wrapper. In the schematization pipeline it gives three sub-agents live access to the target knowledge graph. All three are conditional, so the pipeline still runs with MCP disabled.
questions.flag: Explaining the protocol abstractly. Say what it bought in your system, which was a cheap live pre-check before an expensive subprocess.

teach.title: Where each named thing is actually evidenced

questions.q: What is semantic routing, in your system?
questions.a: Choosing a branch by meaning. The debugger's screener embeds an error log, retrieves the five most similar past incidents, and returns one of three typed categories. That category decides whether the failure is retried, ignored, or investigated. The routing is the expensive decision, not the answer.
questions.flag: Describing it as classification. It is control flow, and framing it that way is what makes the risk visible.

teach.title: Semantic routing, and why it is riskier than it looks

questions.q: What is the riskiest claim on this line?
questions.a: Llama, since no project on the page uses it. GPT is second, because implementing an OpenAI-compatible endpoint is not the same as building on GPT, and a careful reader will make that distinction. Everything else here is backed by a specific system I can describe in detail.
questions.flag: Naming MemGPT. It is genuinely evidenced by the Samsung companion, and undervaluing it wastes a distinctive item.

teach.title: Where each named thing is actually evidenced

questions.q: How does structured output make a system safer?
questions.a: By removing shapes rather than discouraging them. The scout claim schema has no form for an uncited claim, so an uncited claim cannot be emitted. The debug solution's action is a two-value literal, so it cannot return a hedge. A prompt asking for the same thing is advice a model can ignore.
questions.flag: Calling it validation. Validation rejects bad output after the fact. A schema stops it being expressible, and that is a stronger property.

questions.q: When is an agent the wrong answer?
questions.a: Whenever the sequence is known in advance. If you can write the steps down, write them down. An agent is worth it when the path depends on what is found. The debugger's lead manager uses a file finding to direct a code lookup. Most pipelines are not that, including two of mine.
questions.flag: Advocating agents generally. The strongest thing you can say here is where you chose not to use one.

teach.title: The boundary worth defending

questions.q: Give me a framework hook you used for something non-obvious.
questions.a: The before_tool_callback in the lineage agent. The model sometimes called merge before the deterministic extraction had run, producing a graph with zero field mappings and no error. The callback runs extraction if it has not run. That turns a prompt-shaped hope into a precondition.
questions.flag: Naming a hook without the failure it fixed. The failure is what makes it a real answer.

teach.title: Where each named thing is actually evidenced

questions.q: When should tool calls run in sequence, and when in parallel?
questions.a: Sequence when a later call depends on an earlier result, which is what ReAct is. Parallel when they are independent. The vendor Scout runs three model calls concurrently because all three judge the same gathered sources. The debugger's lead manager is sequential because it reasons across tools.
questions.flag: Treating parallel as the better default. Parallel loses cross-tool reasoning, and that loss is exactly why the debugger defaults the other way.

teach.title: The boundary worth defending

questions.q: Why MCP rather than writing the tool yourself?
questions.a: Because a capability described once is usable by every client. Writing it yourself means re-wrapping it per framework, and the wrappers drift. The honest counterpoint is that MCP adds a transport and a dependency. A local function would often do. That is why all three MCP sub-agents in the schematization pipeline are optional.
questions.flag: Selling the protocol. The interesting answer includes why you made it optional.

teach.title: Where each named thing is actually evidenced

questions.q: Why is the router's output a typed literal rather than text?
questions.a: Because the value is control flow. A category parsed out of prose can come back as a fourth thing nobody handled. The handler for that does not exist. A DSPy signature declares three literals and a confidence float. So the router cannot return a branch with no code behind it.
questions.flag: Framing it as convenience. It is the same argument as structured output: remove the shape rather than handle it.

teach.title: Semantic routing, and why it is riskier than it looks

questions.q: Your router always retrieves five incidents. What if nothing is similar?
questions.a: It returns the five least dissimilar things and routes anyway. Top-k always returns k. There is no similarity floor and no nothing-matched branch, so an unfamiliar failure gets a confident category built on loose matches. The fix is a distance threshold that routes to the expensive branch by default.
questions.flag: Assuming a relevance filter exists. It does not, and knowing that about your own retriever is the whole question.

teach.title: Semantic routing, and why it is riskier than it looks

questions.q: How do you choose between model tiers?
questions.a: By what the step is for and who is waiting. Scoring runs on the pro tier because the interview is over, nobody is waiting, and better judgment is worth buying. A live conversational turn uses a faster tier because a person is sitting there. The bake-off in chapter 0001 also showed the cheaper model erring in the more dangerous direction.
questions.flag: Choosing on benchmark scores. The deciding factors are latency tolerance and which direction the errors go.

teach.title: Choosing a model, and pinning it

questions.q: Explain MemGPT's idea in one breath.
questions.a: The model manages its own memory in tiers. A small working context, and a larger external store it pages things in and out of. The model decides what is worth keeping and what to retrieve, so the effective memory is much larger than the context window. It is virtual memory with the model as the pager.
questions.flag: Describing it as RAG. Retrieval is read-only and driven by the query. Here the model also decides what to write, which is the difference.

questions.q: An agent loop grows its context every iteration. What do you do?
questions.a: Compact, and do it by structure rather than by truncation. The schematization retry loop splits feedback on its section headers, drops generation-only sections entirely, and compacts others. Blind truncation is the trap, because it usually cuts the newest errors, which are exactly what the next iteration needs.
questions.flag: Proposing a summarisation call. That adds a model call inside the loop and a new place to lose information.

questions.q: How do you evaluate an agent?
questions.a: Per decision, not end to end. For the router, per-category precision, because a wrong overlook loses a real failure while a wrong retry is self-correcting. For tool use, whether the right tool was chosen. For output, an oracle where one exists. A single end-to-end score averages away the only thing worth knowing.
questions.flag: Proposing one overall accuracy number. The decisions have different costs, so they need different metrics.

teach.title: Semantic routing, and why it is riskier than it looks

questions.q: A tool returns text containing instructions. What stops the model following them?
questions.a: Structurally, nothing. Tool output enters the context as content and the model has no reliable way to tell data from instruction. That is the genuine open problem in agent design. What limits the damage is the boundary. Since my code executes every call, a tool cannot make the system do anything it was not already allowed to do.
questions.flag: Claiming a prompt prevents it. Containment through what tools exist is the real mitigation, not instruction wording.

teach.title: What an agent actually is

questions.q: An agent loops without converging. What stops it?
questions.a: A counter, and it has to be outside the model's reasoning. The debugger's lead manager caps at ten iterations. The schematization loop exits on quality acceptable, quality stagnant, or attempts exhausted. The stagnation exit is the interesting one: stop when the score stops moving, not only when it succeeds.
questions.flag: Relying on the model deciding it is done. That is the thing that has already failed if you are asking the question.

teach.title: Where each named thing is actually evidenced

questions.q: You add a tool and the model never uses it.
questions.a: Almost always the description, not the model. If the description does not clearly say when to reach for it, another tool wins. The second cause is overlap: two tools that sound similar split the choice unpredictably. I would debug it by reading the descriptions as if I were the model, with no other context.
questions.flag: Reaching for a bigger model. It is a documentation bug in a system where documentation is dispatch.

questions.q: How do you handle an agent that gives different answers on identical input?
questions.a: Measure it rather than assume temperature fixes it. In the vendor platform about one claim in five gets a different verdict on identical evidence, and pinning temperature to zero did not fix it. Nearly every flip sits on one category boundary, which points at the prompt's definition rather than at sampling.
questions.flag: Saying temperature zero makes it deterministic. It does not, and having measured that is a much better answer than assuming it.

questions.q: The interviewer asks what you have done with Llama.
questions.a: Say it plainly. Nothing production. It is on the line as familiarity rather than shipped work, and it should either earn a project or come off. The nearest true thing is the on-device work at Samsung over a quantized small model, and that was MobileLLM rather than Llama.
questions.flag: Stretching the Samsung work to cover it. A different model family is a different model family, and the stretch is what gets caught.

teach.title: Where each named thing is actually evidenced

questions.q: And GPT?
questions.a: I would qualify it immediately. What I built is an OpenAI-compatible gateway. So what I know deeply is the API contract: the chat-completions shape, streaming deltas, how tool calls are expressed. Behind that contract I was calling Gemini. That is genuinely useful knowledge, and it is not the same as building on GPT.
questions.flag: Letting it stand unqualified. The gateway detail makes the distinction obvious to anyone who reads the bullet above it.

teach.title: Where each named thing is actually evidenced

questions.q: You have used ADK, CrewAI and DSPy. Does framework knowledge transfer?
questions.a: The concepts do and the details do not. Every one of them has a loop, tools, state and hooks, so the third framework takes days rather than weeks. What does not transfer is the failure modes, and those are what matter. Tool-calling order variance in one, flow routing in another.
questions.flag: Claiming frameworks are interchangeable. The concepts are, and the sharp edges are where all the real time goes.

teach.title: Where each named thing is actually evidenced

questions.q: What would you change about this line?
questions.a: Drop Llama and qualify GPT, so every remaining item is backed by a system I can describe. I would also consider naming DSPy and CrewAI, since both are shipped and neither appears. The line currently names a model I have not used and omits two frameworks I have.
questions.flag: Only adding. The line is long already, and swapping the unbacked items for backed ones is the change that improves it.

teach.title: Where each named thing is actually evidenced

questions.q: A model emits a function call in an agent loop. What actually executes that function?
questions.a:
Your code. The model returns a request naming a function and its arguments, and your process decides whether to honour it. That is why every tool call is a point where you can validate, log or refuse.

Getting this wrong is the most revealing mistake in an LLM interview, because the entire security model follows from it. A tool is not something the model has. It is something you offer, on every single call.
options: Your own code, once the model proposes a call
The model itself, in a sandbox the provider runs
The framework alone, with no code that you control
The provider, on their own side of the network

teach.title: What an agent actually is

questions.q: Semantic routing picks one of three branches. What is the extra risk compared with ordinary retrieval?
questions.a:
The consequence is a different journey, not a worse sentence. In ordinary retrieval a poor chunk gives a slightly worse answer. Here a misleading similar incident can turn an investigate into a retry, so the pipeline reruns and fails again with nobody looking.

A schema cannot catch it, which is the trap in the third option. The schema guarantees the category is one of three valid values. It has no opinion on whether it is the right one.
options: A bad match changes control flow, not just wording
A bad match costs more tokens on every request
A bad match is caught by the schema validator
A bad match only degrades the final answer text

teach.title: Semantic routing, and why it is riskier than it looks

questions.q: “What is an agent, to you?”
questions.a: A model in a loop with tools. It is given typed functions, it proposes a call, my code executes it and returns the result, and it decides again. Without the loop and the tools it is a prompt. The part I would emphasise is that the model never executes anything itself. It emits a request and my process decides whether to honour it, which is where validation, logging and refusal all live.

teach.title: What an agent actually is

questions.q: “Why is that multi-agent rather than three function calls?”
questions.a: In the vendor platform it genuinely is three function calls with one composer, on purpose. Each stage has its own prompt, schema and model tier, which is what makes them worth separating. What it deliberately is not is autonomous: agents never call each other. That restriction is what gives one readable control flow, one place for a deadline, and a stage you can test alone. Agents-calling-agents was rejected, not unavailable.

teach.title: The boundary worth defending

questions.q: “How do you stop an agent doing something dangerous?”
questions.a: By controlling what tools exist, because that bounds what is reachable at all. Then by executing every call in my own code, where I can validate, log or refuse. Then by structured output, so a dangerous instruction has no shape to arrive in. Prompt wording is the weakest layer and I would not lead with it. In the debugger, the strongest control on generated SQL is an allowlist permitting only SELECT and EXPLAIN.

questions.q: “Which of these models have you actually used in production?”
questions.a: Gemini extensively, across every CloudSufi system, including a bake-off between its tiers on a fixed evidence payload. Claude in the pipeline debugger's crews. GPT I would qualify: I built an OpenAI-compatible gateway, so I know the API contract deeply, but the model behind it was Gemini. Llama has no project behind it and I would take it off the line.

teach.title: Where each named thing is actually evidenced

questions.q: “Where did you decide not to use an agent?”
questions.a: In the lineage agent, for the field mappings. Those come out of structured tables, so a parser is correct where a model would be plausible, and the mappings are extracted rather than generated. Also in the schematization pipeline's validation step, which is a subprocess rather than a judge model, because an oracle exists. The rule I use is that a model should only be asked questions with no deterministic answer.
